title: Kummer-root invariance of regular divisor purity
statement:
For a prime $\ell$ and $A=\mathbf F_\ell$, use ordinary small-etale derived categories and Tate twists [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories, def-asd-finite-etale-tate-twist]. If $W$ is a regular Noetherian scheme with $\ell$ invertible [def-weil-regular-scheme], say that $W$ is punctually pure at $w\in W$ when, for $W_w=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{W,w}$, $d_w=\dim\mathcal O_{W,w}$ and its closed-point inclusion $j_w:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(w)\hookrightarrow W_w$, the Kummer fundamental-class map
$$A_{\kappa(w)}\longrightarrow j_w^!A_{W_w}(d_w)[2d_w]$$
of [lem-per-regular-immersion-class-calculus] is an isomorphism. Say that $W$ is punctually pure when this holds at every point. Local rings and residue fields are as in [def-weil-residue-field], affine spectra as in [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and dimension as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be regular Noetherian with $\ell$ invertible, and let $f\in B$ be a nonzerodivisor with $D=\operatorname{Spec}(B/(f))$ regular. Put
$$X'=\operatorname{Spec}B[U]/(U^\ell-f),\qquad D'=V(U)\subset X'.$$
Write $i:D\hookrightarrow X$ and $i':D'\hookrightarrow X'$ [def-weil-closed-immersion], and use polynomial rings as in [def-weil-polynomial-ring]. Then $X'$ is regular, $D'\simeq D$ is a regular effective Cartier divisor, and
$$A_D\to i^!A_X(1)[2]\text{ is an isomorphism}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_{D'}\to i'^!A_{X'}(1)[2]\text{ is an isomorphism}.$$
Empty divisors are allowed. The projection $p:X'\to X$ is finite locally free of rank $\ell$ [def-pc-finite-locally-free], is surjective, and restricts to a surjective etale morphism $X'\setminus D'\to X\setminus D$ [def-weil-etale-morphism].

source.place: Expose XVI Proposition 3.4.5 and its proof, printed pp.246--248 (the monic root algebra, and its Kummer cover away from the divisor).

proof.text: Put $C=B[U]/(U^\ell-f)$ and $u=\overline U$. The monic-quotient basis is $1,u,\ldots,u^{\ell-1}$, so $p$ is finite locally free of rank $\ell$. Every residue-field fibre is a nonzero algebra of dimension $\ell$ over that field and therefore has a prime ideal, proving surjectivity. If $u\sum_{a<\ell}b_au^a=0$, comparison of coefficients gives $b_0=\cdots=b_{\ell-2}=0$ and $fb_{\ell-1}=0$; the last coefficient is zero since $f$ is a nonzerodivisor. Thus $u$ is a nonzerodivisor and $C/(u)=B/(f)$, including the zero ring case. Hence $D'\simeq D$ is a regular effective Cartier divisor. Over $B[1/f]$, $u$ and $\ell$ are units, so the derivative $\ell u^{\ell-1}$ is a unit; the standard monic-derivative presentation proves that the restriction of $p$ is etale, and the same fibre argument proves it surjective.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.246, monic root algebra; elementary coefficient and fibre calculations.

proof.text: At primes containing $u$, apply the root-algebra regularity statement with $R=B$, $n=\ell$ and the given regular quotient $B/(f)$. Off $u$, the preceding etale algebra over the regular ring $B[1/f]$ is regular: apply etale regular-divisor base change to this algebra with divisor equation $1$ (its quotient is the zero regular ring). Thus every local ring of $X'$ is regular. Noetherianity follows from the finite monic presentation over Noetherian $B$. If $D$ is empty, both class maps have zero source and target on the empty etale site and are isomorphisms; all remaining assertions have already been proved. Henceforth test the nonempty divisor at a geometric point $\bar x\to D$.

Write $R=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X,\bar x}$, $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $E=V(f)$ and $V=S\setminus E$. Strict henselizations preserve Noetherianity and regularity. The closed-immersion strict-localization square identifies $R/(f)$ with the strict henselization of the corresponding regular local ring of $D$, so it is regular too. Flatness of the strict henselization and preservation of injections by flat tensor show that $f$ remains a nonzerodivisor. Let $d=\dim R$. The regular-sequence dimension formula gives $\dim R/(f)=d-1$. Lift a minimal set of $d-1$ generators of the maximal ideal of $R/(f)$; together with $f$ they generate the maximal ideal of $R$. They form a regular system of parameters, and in particular $f$ is its first member. This justifies every parameter-root and factorization result used below.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.246, strict-local reduction and the parameter condition; Stacks 06LJ and 04GG as in cited nodes.

proof.text: The factorization statement makes $R$ a domain, makes $f$ prime, and says that the units of $R[1/f]$ are exactly $a f^m$ for $a\in R^\times$ and $m\in\mathbf Z$ (apply its nonnegative-exponent formula to a numerator, then divide by the denominator). Thus $V$ is nonempty connected. Since $R$ is strictly henselian and $\ell$ is invertible, the simple-root lifting criterion applied to $T^\ell-a$ shows that every $a\in R^\times$ is an $\ell$-th power: its nonzero residue has a root in the separably closed residue field, with nonzero derivative. Applying the same criterion to $T^{\ell^2}-1$ lifts a primitive $\ell^2$-th root $\zeta_2$; its powers have pairwise unit differences. Fix $\zeta=\zeta_2^\ell$ to identify $A$ with $\mu_\ell$ on $S$ and $V$. Then $H^0(V,A)=A$ and $R[1/f]^\times/(R[1/f]^\times)^\ell=A$, generated by $f$.

source.place: XVI 3.4.6--3.4.8, p.247, explicit strict-local degree-zero and unit calculation.

proof.text: The Picard vanishing statement for the localization of a regular local ring gives $\operatorname{Pic}(R[1/f])=0$. Hilbert 90 identifies this group with $H^1(V,\mathbf G_m)$. The long exact cohomology sequence of the exact Kummer sequence therefore identifies $H^1(V,\mu_\ell)$ with $R[1/f]^\times/(R[1/f]^\times)^\ell$. In particular it is one-dimensional, generated by the Kummer boundary $\kappa(f)$. This is a calculation, with no assumption of cohomological purity and no assertion about $H^q(V,A)$ for $q\ge2$.

source.place: XVI 3.4.2 and 3.4.8, pp.245--247, reconstructed low-degree Kummer calculation.

proof.text: For the closed immersion $i$, the compactification $(\mathrm{id},i)$ gives $Ri_!=i_*$; uniqueness of right adjoints identifies the class-calculus exceptional adjoint with the closed-support adjoint, including its class morphism. Take the closed-support triangle on $X$ with coefficient $A_X(1)$ at $\bar x$. The qcqs-open strict-henselization stalk formula identifies its third object with $R\Gamma(V,\mu_\ell)$ and its middle object with $A$. Its first object is therefore $\operatorname{Cone}(A\to R\Gamma(V,\mu_\ell))[-1]$. Finite pushforward stalks, applied to the closed immersion, identify this first stalk with the stalk of $i^!A_X(1)$ on $D$. Steps 4--5 and the long exact sequence show that its cohomology vanishes in degrees zero and one, its degree-two group is $A\kappa(f)$ via the boundary, and for $q\ge3$ its degree-$q$ group is $H^{q-1}(V,\mu_\ell)$. Class calculus identifies the class map with the transpose $\eta_D$ of the supported Kummer morphism $c_{D,A}$, and the supported-Kummer localization-boundary statement gives $\eta_D=\pm\partial\kappa(f)$ for the boundary $\partial$ of this closed-support triangle. Geometric stalks are exact and carry the triangle and its boundary to the stalk triangle, sending $\kappa(f)$ to its restriction to $V$; so the class-map stalk sends $1$ to $\pm$ the generator of Steps 4--5. Hence the class-map stalk after shift $[2]$ is an isomorphism exactly when $H^q(V,A)=0$ for every $q\ge2$. Stalks commute with cohomology, and geometric stalks detect sheaf isomorphisms. Testing this at all $\bar x\to D$ therefore tests the global class map. This proves the required strict-local test directly.

source.place: XVI Proposition 3.4.2 and Lemma 3.4.8, pp.245--247; Stacks 03Q9 (theorem-higher-direct-images) and 0A45 (lemma-cohomology-with-support-triangle).

proof.text: For $a=1,2$ form $R_a=R[t_a]/(t_a^{\ell^a}-f)$ and $V_a=\operatorname{Spec}R_a[1/t_a]$, with $t_1=t_2^\ell$. The henselian parameter-root regularity statement gives strictly henselian regular local rings $R_a$, residue field equal to that of $R$, and parameter $t_a$. The quotient $R_a/(t_a)=R/(f)$ is regular. The finite-base strict-localization statement, and the fact that the closed fibre is the local algebra $\kappa(\bar x)[t_1]/(t_1^\ell)$ with one geometric point, identify $\operatorname{Spec}R_1$ with the strict localization of $X'$ at the unique point over $\bar x$. Consequently the calculations of Steps 4--6 apply to $(R_1,t_1)$ as well. The class-map test for $X'$ at this point is exactly $H^{\ge2}(V_1,A)=0$, whereas that for $X$ is $H^{\ge2}(V,A)=0$.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, pp.246--247, regular local root algebras and the first two levels of the tower.

proof.text: The rotations $t_2\mapsto\zeta_2^b t_2$ make $V_2\to V$ a torsor for $C_2=\mathbf Z/\ell^2\mathbf Z$, and $g:V_1\to V$ its quotient torsor for $Q=\mathbf Z/\ell\mathbf Z$. Indeed all maps are finite free, surjective and etale by the same monic and derivative calculation as Step 1. After adjoining a root, the polynomial factors as $\prod_b(T-\zeta_2^b t_2)$; distinct roots differ by units. Evaluation identifies the algebra with the product of its factors, with inverse given by the interpolation idempotents $\prod_{c\ne b}(T-\zeta_2^c t_2)/(\zeta_2^b t_2-\zeta_2^c t_2)$. This proves the torsor identity and its compatibility with $t_1=t_2^\ell$. Put $M=g_*A$. On the etale cover $V_2$, it is the constant vector space $\operatorname{Map}(Q,A)$ with the cyclic translation descent action.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.247, Kummer root tower; explicit torsor calculation.

proof.text:
The associated-module functor for $V_2\to V$ is exact: after restricting to that etale covering it is the constant-sheaf functor on vector spaces, which is exact because exact sequences of vector spaces split; exactness descends since geometric stalks on a surjective etale cover detect kernels and cokernels. It takes the trivial representation $A$ to $A_V$ and the inflated permutation representation to $M$. The exact-functor derived factorization therefore applies the cyclic-square splitting to give
$$[M\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}M]\simeq A_V\oplus A_V[-1]\quad\text{in }D(V_{\mathrm{et}},A),$$
with the complex in degrees zero and one and $\sigma$ a cyclic generator. This is the only new homological input; it says nothing about purity or cohomology of $V$.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.248, finite permutation-module argument; agent finite-level derived splitting in place of the relative-functor formulation.

proof.text: Suppose $H^q(V,A)=0$ for $q\ge2$. In the permutation representation, the cyclic operator $z=\sigma-1$ identifies the underlying module with $A[z]/(z^\ell)$: a delta-function is a cyclic vector, and $(\sigma-1)^\ell=\sigma^\ell-1=0$. The filtration by $z^a$ has $\ell$ successive one-dimensional trivial quotients. Applying the exact associated-module functor gives a filtration of $M$ with constant quotients $A_V$. The long exact sequence for each short exact filtration step, starting with zero, gives $H^q(V,M)=0$ for every $q\ge2$. Finite direct image is exact, and derived pushforward composition with global sections identifies $R\Gamma(V,M)$ with $R\Gamma(V_1,A)$. Thus $H^{\ge2}(V_1,A)=0$.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.248, trivial-quotient filtration and the forward implication.

proof.text:
Conversely suppose $H^{\ge2}(V_1,A)=0$. Exact finite direct image and derived pushforward composition give $H^{\ge2}(V,M)=0$. Write $L=R\Gamma(V,M)$ and $K=[M\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}M]$ in degrees zero and one, so $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\sigma-1)[-1]$. Derived global sections is triangulated; hence
$$R\Gamma(V,K)\simeq\operatorname{Cone}(L\xrightarrow{\sigma-1}L)[-1].$$
Its long exact sequence has zero groups in every degree $r\ge3$, since $H^r(L)=H^{r-1}(L)=0$ there. On the other hand Step 9 gives
$$H^r(V,K)\simeq H^r(V,A)\oplus H^{r-1}(V,A).$$
Taking $r=q+1\ge3$ makes $H^q(V,A)$ a direct summand of zero. This proves $H^{\ge2}(V,A)=0$ without any finite-dimensionality assumption on these groups and without selecting cones functorially.

source.place: XVI 3.4.5, p.248, reverse implication; agent finite-level splitting argument using the second Kummer root.

proof.text: Steps 10--11 identify the two vanishing tests of Step 7 for each geometric point of $D\simeq D'$. Step 6 identifies each test with invertibility of the corresponding geometric stalk of the specified Kummer class map. Therefore one global class map is invertible if and only if the other is. Together with Steps 1--2 this proves every clause of the item, including the empty-divisor case.
